  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications</h1>
<span class="ltx_pubnotes ltx_pubnotes_meta"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_conference"><span class="ltx_note_name">Conference: </span>Proc. of the 25th International Conference

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">When training artificial intelligence (AI) to perform tasks, humans often care not only about <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">whether</span> a task is completed but also <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how</span> it is performed.
As AI agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, aligning their behavior with human-provided specifications becomes critical for responsible AI deployment.
<span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Reward design</span> provides a direct channel for such alignment by translating human expectations into reward functions that guide reinforcement learning (RL).
However, existing methods are often too limited to capture nuanced human preferences that arise in long-horizon tasks.
Hence, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hierarchical Reward Design from Language (HRDL)</span>: a problem formulation that extends classical reward design to encode richer behavioral specifications for hierarchical RL agents.
We further propose <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Language to Hierarchical Rewards (L2HR)</span> as a solution to HRDL.
Experiments show that AI agents trained with rewards designed via L2HR not only complete tasks effectively but also better adhere to human specifications.
Together, HRDL and L2HR advance the research on human-aligned AI agents.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Reward Design; Human-Centered AI; Hierarchical RL
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h3>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18582v1/overview.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:613/207;" width="613" height="207" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This work introduces the Hierarchical Reward Design from Language (HRDL) problem. Unlike prior work on reward design, HRDL decomposes reward design into low- and high-level components <math id="S1.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{L},\tilde{r}_{H})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{L},\tilde{r}_{H})</annotation></semantics></math>. Language to Hierarchical Rewards (L2HR), our proposed solution to HRDL, leverages language models to guide the synthesis of these hierarchical rewards, enabling existing RL algorithms to train agents that are better aligned with human specifications.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Robots and other AI agents are increasingly being deployed in human-centric environments, such as homes, hospitals, and disaster zones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scopelliti et al., 2004</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kidd and Breazeal, 2008</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pantofaru et al., 2012</a>; <a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unhelkar et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unhelkar et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez-Aguirre et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Seo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Their usefulness depends not only on task completion, but also on respecting human intentions, operational rules, and safety requirements (collectively referred to as <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">behavior specifications</span>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Aligning agent behavior with these specifications is central to their responsible deployment, with various paradigms being actively explored for conveying such specifications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chernova and Thomaz, 2022</a>)</cite>.
This work focuses on <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reward design</span>, a paradigm where humans convey specifications through reward functions that guide reinforcement learning (RL), typically before AI deployment.
This paradigm is particularly suitable for use cases where specifications are relatively stable and the costs of reward design can be amortized, such as during the repeated use of AI agents by humans in domain-specific contexts.
<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup>
            
            
            
            
            
            
          This article is an extended version of an identically-titled paper accepted at the <span id="footnote1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)</span>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As AI agents take on increasingly complex tasks, more advanced reward design methods are needed to capture equally complex specifications.
Humans rarely reason about tasks and associated specifications as monolithic goals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miller et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Botvinick et al., 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Correa et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Catrambone, 1998</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramaraj, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2013</a>)</cite>.
Instead, we naturally break them into subtasks.
Hierarchical frameworks in RL mirror this structure by decomposing tasks into subtasks and organizing them over long horizons <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dayan and Hinton, 1992</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parr and Russell, 1997</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton et al., 1999</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dietterich, 2000</a>)</cite>.
This <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hierarchical approach to policy learning</span> has enabled agents to complete tasks of increasingly longer horizons.
However, <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">the reward design for these hierarchical RL agents remains largely unexplored,</span> thereby limiting human-AI alignment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1. Introduction ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, specifications for long-horizon tasks often include details on <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">what</span> subtasks to perform, in <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">which</span> order, and <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how</span> they are executed.
Existing reward design methods encode these specifications via a flat reward function of the form <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>.
We show <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">theoretically and empirically that flat rewards are fundamentally limited in capturing specifications for long-horizon tasks</span>.
To address this limitation:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce the <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hierarchical Reward Design (HRD)</span> problem, which enables designers to express behavioral specifications inspired by the same structured way people naturally think and teach. Unlike the classical (flat) reward design problem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, HRD admits reward solutions that enable encoding of complex specifications for long-horizon tasks, capturing both what subtasks to perform and how to execute them. HRD is a general formulation that can be instantiated with multiple input modalities, analogous to how flat reward design has been realized via proxy signals or language <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Because natural language is an intuitive medium for specifying layered instructions, we then provide a language-based instantiation called <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hierarchical Reward Design from Language (HRDL, pronounced “hurdle”)</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We prove that hierarchical rewards of HRDL are strictly more expressive than flat rewards used by prior works, while remaining compatible with standard decision-making frameworks (i.e. Markov and semi-Markov Decision Processes) and RL algorithms.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Language to Hierarchical Rewards (L2HR)</span>, an initial solution to HRDL that generates hierarchical rewards directly from natural language specifications, making reward design more accessible while leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang and Chang, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. L2HR produces reward structures that guide both high-level subtask selection and low-level execution.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Human subject and numerical experiments demonstrate hierarchical reward design’s advantages over flat reward design.
Hierarchical reward design (coupled with hierarchical RL) enables AI agents to successfully complete tasks and better align their behavior with language specifications.
We view this work as an initial but important step toward aligning AI systems with human expectations through the lens of HRD.
Through theoretical analysis and empirical findings, this paper lays the groundwork for future research on designing human-aligned reward structures that employ hierarchies and human input.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Background and Related Work</h3>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work focuses on AI agents tasked with sequential decision-making tasks, which are commonly modeled using Markov Decision Processes (MDP) or its variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Puterman, 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton and Barto, 2018</a>)</cite>.
An MDP is defined by the tuple <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}\doteq(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>≐</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}\doteq(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r,\gamma,h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r,\gamma,h)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> are the state and action spaces, <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(s^{\prime}|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(s^{\prime}|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> the transition dynamics, <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> the reward function, <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> the discount factor, and <math id="S2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> the horizon.
MDPs can be solved using RL, which aims to find a policy <math id="S2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math> that maximizes the expected discounted return <math id="S2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t=0}^{h}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>h</mi></msubsup><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t=0}^{h}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While capable, standard RL algorithms struggle with long-horizon tasks.
Hierarchical RL (HRL) seeks to solve MDPs with long horizons by decomposing them into simpler subtasks  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dayan and Hinton, 1992</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parr and Russell, 1997</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton et al., 1999</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dietterich, 2000</a>; <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Seo and Unhelkar, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Seo and Unhelkar, 2025</a>)</cite>.
A widely used HRL paradigm is the options framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton et al., 1999</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bacon et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Whiteson, 2019</a>)</cite>.
Here, the agent has access to a discrete set of temporally-extended behaviors called options <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Each <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> is associated with an intra-option policy <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{L}(a|s,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{L}(a|s,o)</annotation></semantics></math> and a termination condition <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta(o^{-},s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>o</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta(o^{-},s)</annotation></semantics></math>.
A high-level policy <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{H}(o|o^{-},s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><msup><mi>o</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{H}(o|o^{-},s)</annotation></semantics></math> selects options, while the low-level policy executes primitive actions until the selected option terminates.
The reward model for options computes the expected cumulative reward until option termination.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton et al., 1999</a>)</cite>, we let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}(o,s,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}(o,s,t)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the event where option <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math> is initiated in state <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> at timestep <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, and define the option-level reward as:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_gather ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle r_{opt}(s,o)\doteq\mathbb{E}[\Sigma_{i=1}^{k}\gamma^{i-1}r_{t+i}\mid\mathcal{E}(o,s,t)]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≐</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle r_{opt}(s,o)\doteq\mathbb{E}[\Sigma_{i=1}^{k}\gamma^{i-1}r_{t+i}\mid\mathcal{E}(o,s,t)]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of steps after which the initiated option <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math> terminates, determined by its termination condition <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Another line of HRL research follows the <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">feudal/goal-conditioned framework</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dayan and Hinton, 1992</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vezhnevets et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kulkarni et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nachum et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, which also decomposes a task into subtasks but differs in how the hierarchical policies are trained and how reward signals are assigned.
In this framework, the high-level manager selects subgoals and receives a <em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task</em> reward, as in the options framework.
However, unlike the options framework, the low-level worker receives a separate <em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pseudo-reward</em> <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{p}(s,o,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{p}(s,o,a)</annotation></semantics></math> that measures progress toward achieving the current subgoal.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>Reward Design</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A core challenge in using MDPs and RL is reward design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton and Barto, 2018</a>)</cite>.
Given a well-designed reward function, agents can use RL algorithms to solve the MDP.
However, in practice, the design of a reward function is non-trivial and can lead to a host of problems, including poor alignment between humans and agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amodei et al., 2016</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.1. </span>Reward Design Problem.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To formally study reward design, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al.</a></cite> introduce the (flat) Reward Design Problem (RDP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2009</a>)</cite>.
RDP is formalized as a tuple <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=(\mathcal{M}_{p},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}},F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=(\mathcal{M}_{p},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}},F)</annotation></semantics></math>, where</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma,h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma,h)</annotation></semantics></math> is the <span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">world model</span>;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is the space of reward functions;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r):\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\Pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r):\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\Pi</annotation></semantics></math> is an algorithm to compute policy <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{A})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{A})</annotation></semantics></math> that optimizes reward <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\in\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\in\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math> in the MDP <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{M}_{p},r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{M}_{p},r)</annotation></semantics></math>; and</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F:\Pi\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F:\Pi\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is the fitness function that produces a scalar evaluation of a policy, only accessible via policy queries.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The RDP seeks a reward function <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\in\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\in\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">the policy <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi:=\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi:=\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r)</annotation></semantics></math> that optimizes <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math></span> achieves the highest Fitness score <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(\pi)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Rather than treating the reward as fixed and exogenous, RDP reframes reward design as a <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">search problem</span>, a perspective that has profoundly shaped subsequent research.
It inspired methods that optimize or evolve reward functions directly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sorg et al., 2010a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niekum et al., 2010</a>)</cite> as well as formulations that infer or generate them from indirect signals, such as Inverse Reward Design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, which recovers true rewards from proxy rewards, and Eureka <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which synthesizes executable rewards from natural language.
Many other paradigms can be viewed as RDP instantiations: inverse RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abbeel and Ng, 2004</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ziebart et al., 2008</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho and Ermon, 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2018</a>)</cite> treats expert behavior as evidence for the reward search, while preference-based learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sadigh et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Basu et al., 2018</a>)</cite> and RLHF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2022</a>)</cite> extend this to human feedback.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S2.F2.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="95.04" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 274.17 95.04" <section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.2. </span>Rewards Design for Hierarchical RL.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While RDP provides a unifying framework that has catalyzed advances in both RL and human-AI alignment, <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">it does not explicitly consider hierarchical RL</span>.
Many prior works have explored the use of hierarchical rewards, from early studies in feudal reinforcement learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dayan and Hinton, 1992</a>)</cite> and precursors to the options framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh, 1992</a>)</cite> to more recent advances in deep HRL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vezhnevets et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kulkarni et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nachum et al., 2018</a>)</cite>.
While these works often <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">assume access</span> to hierarchical rewards for training agents to complete tasks, <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">the problem of <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">designing</span> such hierarchical rewards has received little attention and, to our knowledge, has yet to be formally defined as a concrete research problem</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A literature search using the keywords “hierarchical reward design” primarily returns domain-specific studies that discuss how <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">using</span> hierarchical rewards enables solving application-level problems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Newton et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naito et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Other works either employ the term <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hierarchy</span> in different contexts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, such as to express the relative importance of multiple flat reward signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
A related but conceptually distinct line of work utilizes Reward Machines (RMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Icarte et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Furelos-Blanco et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which represent rewards using automata or temporal logic.
RM-based approaches focus on exploiting known reward structures to improve <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">learning efficiency</span>, rather than on studying how such structures can be specified from human input.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Since no previous work formally defines the <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">design of hierarchical rewards</span> as a general problem, there is a lack of consistent language and theoretical foundation for studying it.
This work addresses this gap at the intersection of hierarchical rewards and reward design (Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.2.1. Reward Design Problem. ‣ 2.2. Reward Design ‣ 2. Background and Related Work ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) by formalizing the Hierarchical Reward Design problem and introducing a reward structure that is hierarchical, compact, and capable of capturing nuanced behavioral specifications for both <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">what</span> subtasks to select and <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how</span> to execute them.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Just as RDP lays the groundwork for studying algorithmic reward design in flat settings, we posit that HRD will provide a principled foundation for reasoning about hierarchical reward structures.</span> In line with the research that originated from RDP, we anticipate that HRD will enable a broad range of problem instantiations (of reward design with different types of human inputs) and solution methods for designing hierarchical rewards.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.3. </span>Reward Design from Language.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early work addressing the RDP focused on designing rewards for intrinsic motivation and reward shaping <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2010</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sorg et al., 2010b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sorg et al., 2010a</a>)</cite>.
More recently, research in this area has explored aligning agent behavior more closely with human-provided specifications, using learning or large language models (LLMs) to infer and generate reward functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
In these cases, the human or an oracle, either implicitly or explicitly, serves as the fitness function by evaluating the policy.
However, most existing work on reward design or generation focuses exclusively on non-hierarchical (flat) RL settings, producing reward functions of the form <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{flat}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{flat}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2010</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sorg et al., 2010b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sorg et al., 2010a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhambri et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
While sufficient for certain behaviors, <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">flat reward functions are fundamentally limited when specifying complex preferences, such as desired subtask sequences or option-conditioned execution strategies, that naturally arise in long-horizon tasks</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To our knowledge, the only prior work that explicitly considers a hierarchical setting is <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Masadome and Harada, 2025</a>)</cite>, though its focus differs substantially from ours.
Their approach does not formalize the hierarchical reward design problem or analyze the expressivity gap between flat and hierarchical formulations.
Moreover, the rewards generated by their LLMs are limited to task completion objectives and do not capture behavioral specifications.
In contrast, L2HR generates both high- and low-level rewards that encode natural language behavioral preferences while preserving task feasibility.<span id="footnote1a" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Please see the Appendix for additional details on related works.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Hierarchical Reward Design</h3>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section formally introduces the Hierarchical Reward Design problem.
We begin by defining the low- and high-level reward functions in HRD and proceed to show that they naturally induce a family of MDPs at the low-level and a semi-MDP (SMDP) at the high-level.
Using these insights, we formally define the general HRD problem along with a specific instantiation, the <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hierarchical Reward Design from Language (HRDL)</span> problem.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Proofs for all propositions are also provided in the Appendix.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Low<span id="S3.SS1.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>level and High-level Reward Models</h4>

<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Definition 0 (Low-level Reward).</h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The <span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">low-level reward</span> is a function
<math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{L}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{L}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, which provides feedback for selecting a low-level action <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a\in\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\in\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> in state <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> while pursuing option <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{L}(s,o,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{L}(s,o,a)</annotation></semantics></math> encodes specifications for <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how</span> the agent should execute the subtask associated with option <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math> in state <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Proposition 0 (Low-level MDP Models).</h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma)</annotation></semantics></math> be a world model, <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> a set of options, and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{L}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{L}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> a low<span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text">-</span>level reward.
For a fixed option <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>, the tuple <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{L,o}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,r_{L}(\cdot,o,\cdot),\gamma,h_{o})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{L,o}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,r_{L}(\cdot,o,\cdot),\gamma,h_{o})</annotation></semantics></math> defines an MDP, where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> is the horizon determined by the option’s termination condition <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta(\cdot,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta(\cdot,o)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Definition 0 (High-level Reward).</h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The <span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">high-level reward</span> is a function
<math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{H}:\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{H}:\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, which specifies the expected reward for executing option <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> until termination, given that <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math> is initiated in state <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and the previous option was <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o^{-}\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>o</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o^{-}\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The high-level reward <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{H}(o^{-},s,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>o</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{H}(o^{-},s,o)</annotation></semantics></math> encodes specifications for <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">what</span> subtask should be executed, possibly conditioned on both the current state and prior option.
This allows for expressing preferences over subtask <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ordering</span> and dependencies between subtasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Proposition 0 (High-level SMDP Model).</h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let </span><math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma,h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma,h)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> be a world model, </span><math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> a set of options, and </span><math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{H}:\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{H}:\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> the high</span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">-</span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">level reward. Then, </span><math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{H}=(\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S},\mathcal{O},T_{H},r_{H},\gamma,h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{H}=(\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S},\mathcal{O},T_{H},r_{H},\gamma,h)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> forms a semi-MDP, where </span><math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{H}:\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>ℕ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{H}:\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N})</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> defines the joint distribution over the next augmented state and transit time, where </span><math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is the set of natural numbers.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Alternatively, the high-level process can be modeled as a standard MDP when <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">single-step</span> high-level rewards are used.
This flexibility highlights that the HRD framework is compatible with both semi-MDP and MDP formulations, allowing the use of a wide range of existing RL algorithms.
We provide the formal MDP definition and corresponding proofs in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>The HRD Problem</h4>

<div id="S3.Thmtheorem5" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Definition 0 (Hierarchical Reward Design (HRD)).</h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The <span id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hierarchical Reward Design (HRD)</span> problem is defined by the tuple <math id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=(\mathcal{M}_{p},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}},F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=(\mathcal{M}_{p},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}},F)</annotation></semantics></math>, where</span></p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma,h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{p}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,\gamma,h)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is the world model;</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is a finite option set;</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}_{H}\times\mathcal{R}_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}_{H}\times\mathcal{R}_{L}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is the space of candidate reward structures, where </span><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}_{H}=\{r_{H}:\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi </div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

</span><math id="S3.I1.i4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{L}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> in each underlying MDP </span><math id="S3.I1.i4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math"
