</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">the fitness function </span><math id="S3.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F:\Pi_{H}\times\Pi_{L}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F:\Pi_{H}\times\Pi_{L}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> evaluates the quality of hierarchical policies.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The goal of HRD is to find <math id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(r_{H}^{*},r_{L}^{*})=\arg\max_{(r_{H},r_{L})\in\mathcal{R}}F(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r_{H},r_{L}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(r_{H}^{*},r_{L}^{*})=\arg\max_{(r_{H},r_{L})\in\mathcal{R}}F(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r_{H},r_{L}))</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Connections to Existing Algorithms.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show in the Appendix that <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be instantiated with existing RL algorithms.
In our implementation, the low-level policy <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{L}(a\mid s,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{L}(a\mid s,o)</annotation></semantics></math> is trained with PPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017</a>)</cite> due to its robustness in control, while the high-level policy <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{H}(o\mid o^{-},s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msup><mi>o</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{H}(o\mid o^{-},s)</annotation></semantics></math> uses DQN-style methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mnih et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, following common practice in SMDP formulations  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton et al., 1999</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bacon et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.
Stronger structural assumptions on <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(r_{H},r_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(r_{H},r_{L})</annotation></semantics></math> can enable the use of more specialized HRL algorithms.
For instance, if the low-level reward depends only on state and action, <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{L}(s,o,a)=r_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{L}(s,o,a)=r_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the high-level reward <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{H}</annotation></semantics></math> is a single-step reward constructed as <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{a}r_{flat}(s,a)\pi_{L}(a|s,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{a}r_{flat}(s,a)\pi_{L}(a|s,o)</annotation></semantics></math>, the problem reduces to the two augmented MDPs formulation introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Whiteson, 2019</a>)</cite>.
In these cases, algorithms such as double actor-critic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Whiteson, 2019</a>)</cite> and option-critic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bacon et al., 2017</a>)</cite> can be applied to learn hierarchical policies.
A detailed exploration of the connections between structural reward assumptions and the applicability of existing HRL algorithms for instantiating <math id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}</annotation></semantics></math> is left for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Hierarchical Reward Design from Language</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As discussed in Sec. <a href="#S1" title="1. Introduction ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, real-world deployments often require agents to satisfy additional behavioral specifications beyond task completion.
In these cases, the task reward can typically be defined once and reused across different behavioral contexts.
In contrast, additional rewards must be redesigned for each new behavior specification.
While the cost of task reward design is amortized, the cost of designing rewards that match human specifications grows linearly with the number of distinct behaviors desired.
This motivates the need for an automated approach to generate rewards to encode behavioral specifications while reusing the existing domain dynamics and task objectives.
The challenge of this problem is twofold:
(1) The generated rewards should have distinct functional forms – one guiding high-level option selection, and another governing low-level action execution.
(2) The generated rewards must remain compatible with existing task rewards, ensuring that agents continue to achieve the original task objectives.
We formally define this as a specific instantiation of the HRD problem.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem6" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Definition 0 (Hierarchical Reward Design from Language (HRDL)).</h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The <span id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HRDL</span> problem is an instance of the HRD problem with additional inputs: (1) a task reward function <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, (2) a subtask completion reward (pseudo-reward) <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{p}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{p}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, and (3) behavior specifications <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l\in\Sigma^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l\in\Sigma^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, provided as a natural language description.
<math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> guides the reward generation during training, and the fitness function <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> is accessible <span id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">only</span> during evaluation.
The objective of HRDL is to generate high- and low-level designed rewards, <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}=(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})\in\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}=(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})\in\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that the resulting hierarchical policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\pi_{H}^{*},\pi_{L}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\pi_{H}^{*},\pi_{L}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math>, trained under the composite rewards <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(r_{opt}+\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},r_{p}+\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(r_{opt}+\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},r_{p}+\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math> using <math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}</annotation></semantics></math>, maximizes the fitness score:
<math id="S3.Thmtheorem6.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})=\arg\max_{(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})\in\mathcal{R}}F(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r_{opt}+\tilde{r}_{H},r_{p}+\tilde{r}_{L}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})=\arg\max_{(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})\in\mathcal{R}}F(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(r_{opt}+\tilde{r}_{H},r_{p}+\tilde{r}_{L}))</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">If a <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">non-hierarchical</span> reward design method is used, the designed reward has the flat form <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>.
To integrate this flat reward into the hierarchical setting, we must decompose it into high- and low-level rewards:</p>

<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat,H}(s,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat,H}(s,o)</annotation></semantics></math> aggregates <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> using the same expression as Eq. <a href="#S2.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 2.1. Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning ‣ 2. Background and Related Work ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
While flat designed rewards <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> can encode some behavior specifications, the definitions of high- and low-level rewards in HRD provide a significantly more expressive mechanism for specifying agent behavior:</p>

<p id="S3.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">In fact, the flat reward is a special case of hierarchically designed rewards, where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{L}(s,o,a)=\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{L}(s,o,a)=\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{H}(o^{-},s,o)=\tilde{r}_{flat,H}(s,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>o</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{H}(o^{-},s,o)=\tilde{r}_{flat,H}(s,o)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The hierarchical formulation is strictly more general than the flat formulation, offering greater expressiveness in the following ways:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproperty1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_property">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Property 1.</h6>
<div id="Thmproperty1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproperty1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproperty1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Certain specifications on sub-task selection can be expressed through <math id="Thmproperty1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{H}(s,o^{-},o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>o</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{H}(s,o^{-},o)</annotation></semantics></math>, but they cannot be expressed by flat function: <math id="Thmproperty1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmproperty2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_property">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_smallcaps ltx_title_theorem">Property 2.</h6>
<div id="Thmproperty2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproperty2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproperty2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Certain specifications on sub-task execution can be expressed through <math id="Thmproperty2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{L}(s,o,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{L}(s,o,a)</annotation></semantics></math>, but they cannot be expressed by flat function: <math id="Thmproperty2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Proofs of these properties are provided in the Appendix.
In the following sections, we introduce an algorithm for generating hierarchical rewards <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})</annotation></semantics></math> from natural language specifications and empirically compare its performance against flat reward design that generates alignment rewards of the form <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Language to Hierarchical Rewards (L2HR)</h3>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now present L2HR, an algorithm designed to solve HRDL by leveraging large language models (LLMs).
L2HR represents reward functions as programs, which it generates directly from natural language specifications.
Specifically, it first employs a structured prompting strategy to capture specifications as prompts, which are then used as inputs to a training module that produces hierarchical reward functions.
An illustration of L2HR’s input and output is provided in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2. Training Procedure ‣ 4. Language to Hierarchical Rewards (L2HR) ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, with more details available in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>Prompting Strategy</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To generate executable reward functions from natural language, L2HR requires the specifications to be provided as a structured prompt.
We design a prompting strategy for L2HR inspired by Eureka, a recent approach for LLM-based reward generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, unlike Eureka, L2HR’s prompt design focuses on producing feasible reward functions without relying on access to a fitness <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> during reward code generation.
Specifically, within L2HR, the LLM is provided with a structured prompt comprising:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Task Description</span>:
A natural language description of the overall task objective, including the approximate scale of the task reward.
Since RL is sensitive to reward magnitudes, this information helps ensure that the generated preference rewards are neither too small to influence learning nor so large as to destabilize training.
The task reward code itself is intentionally withheld to reflect realistic settings in which only the reward signal (but not the code) is accessible and to prevent overfitting to implementation details.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Environment Code Context</span>:
Snippets of environment source code that expose the state and action spaces without revealing simulation internals, following the methodology of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(3)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Relevant Action-Related Spaces</span>: Descriptions of the option space <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> and action space <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, including the semantic role of each. We include these descriptions to help the LLM correctly distinguish between high-level and low-level decision spaces.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(4)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Behavior Specification</span>: A natural language string that describes the desired agent behaviors beyond task completion.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(5)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Formatting and Reward Design Tips</span>:
Coding constraints (e.g., avoiding global variables) and guidance on balancing designed rewards with the underlying task reward.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span>Training Procedure</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given the structured prompt, state-of-the-art LLMs can generate plausible reward code in a zero-shot manner.
However, we find that zero-shot generation often yields reward code with syntax errors and invalid variable references in practice.
To mitigate these issues, L2HR incorporates a training procedure for reward code generation that couples LLMs with RL.
Specifically, L2HR generates <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> reward candidates independently from the LLM and apply a lightweight filtering process to ensure validity.
During filtering, L2HR verifies whether the code compiles without syntax errors, and whether it references only permitted state, option, and action variables exposed in the environment prompt.
We find that at least one sample in the batch passes these checks.
As a result, we forego more complex iterative refinement strategies, such as evolutionary search or reward reflection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, leaving their integration into L2HR as a direction for future work.</p>
</div>

</span>
<span id="lstnumberx8" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    </span><span id="lstnumberx8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Tuple</span><span id="lstnumberx8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">[</span><span id="lstnumberx8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_lst_keywords2 ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">float</span><span id="lstnumberx8.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx8.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx8.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Dict</span><span id="lstnumberx8.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">[</span><span id="lstnumberx8.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_lst_keywords2 ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">str</span><span id="lstnumberx8.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx8.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx8.12" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_lst_keywords2 ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">float</span><span id="lstnumberx8.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">]]:</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx9" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    </span><span id="lstnumberx9.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">…</span>

<span id="lstnumberx10" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    </span><span id="lstnumberx10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">return</span><span id="lstnumberx10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">reward</span><span id="lstnumberx10.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx10.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx10.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">reward_components</span>

</span><span id="lstnumberx13.14" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_lst_keywords2 ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">int</span><span id="lstnumberx13.15" class="ltx_text" </span>
<span id="lstnumberx15" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx15.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    </span><span id="lstnumberx15.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">…</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx16" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx16.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    </span><span id="lstnumberx16.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">return</span><span id="lstnumberx16.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx16.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">reward</span><span id="lstnumberx16.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx16.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx16.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">reward_components</span>
</span>

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>. </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Illustration of L2HR input and output.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The full two-stage training procedure of <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">L2HR</span> is provided in the Appendix.
In the first stage, L2HR uses the LLM to generate <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> candidate low-level alignment functions <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{L}^{(1)},\dots,\tilde{r}_{L}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{L}^{(1)},\dots,\tilde{r}_{L}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> from the specification <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>.
The low-level prompt differs from the high-level one only in its description of the action space and level-specific behavior specifications.
Each <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{L}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{L}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> is then used to train a corresponding low-level policy <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{L}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{L}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> with the combined objective of pseudo-rewards plus the LLM-generated <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{L}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{L}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Only the policies <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{L}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{L}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> that surpass a predefined threshold of subgoal completion, based on cumulative pseudo-rewards, are considered as <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">valid</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the second stage, L2HR generates <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> candidate high-level alignment functions <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{H}^{(1)},\dots,\tilde{r}_{H}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{H}^{(1)},\dots,\tilde{r}_{H}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> and uses them to train high-level policies <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{H}^{(j)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{H}^{(j)}</annotation></semantics></math>, each conditioned on a <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">valid</span> <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{L}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{L}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> from the first stage.
These policies are optimized using with the combined objective of option-level task reward plus the LLM-generated <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{H}^{(j)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{H}^{(j)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then, L2HR returns all designed rewards <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{H}^{(j)},\tilde{r}_{L}^{(i)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{H}^{(j)},\tilde{r}_{L}^{(i)})</annotation></semantics></math> and corresponding trained policy pairs <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\pi_{H}^{(j)},\pi_{L}^{(i)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\pi_{H}^{(j)},\pi_{L}^{(i)})</annotation></semantics></math> that achieve cumulative task rewards above a threshold.
This two-stage structure promotes modularity and allows for selective reuse of subtask policies.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5. </span>Experiments</h3>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We empirically evaluate whether framing reward generation as a hierarchical problem offers advantages over the traditional flat (non-hierarchical) formulation.
Specifically, we aim to evaluate:</p>
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S5.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q1</span>.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Are the generated alignment rewards syntactically correct?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S5.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q2</span>.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Do they preserve task feasibility?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S5.I1.i3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q3</span>.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Do they successfully induce behaviors that match the provided specifications?</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">To investigate <span id="S5.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q3</span>, we additionally conduct user studies.
The Appendix includes further experimental details, including
more information about the domains, metrics, LLM prompts, hyperparameters, and user study protocol.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1. </span>Baselines</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate L2HR (referred to as <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> in the tables), we consider the following baselines.
For all LLM-based experiments, we generate <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=8</annotation></semantics></math> reward function candidates per trial using GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and repeat this process 3 times, resulting in a total of 24 reward candidates per configuration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Language to Flat Reward (Flat).</span>
This baseline generates flat alignment reward <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> from language and incorporates it into the hierarchical setting using Eq. <a href="#S3.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ 3.3. Hierarchical Reward Design from Language ‣ 3. Hierarchical Reward Design ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and  <a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.3. Hierarchical Reward Design from Language ‣ 3. Hierarchical Reward Design ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> to maintain a consistent two-level training framework.
Prompts are identical to those used for L2HR, except that the prompts for flat reward generation exclude option-related instructions (since flat rewards are independent of options) and express user preferences as a single combined description rather than separate high- and low-level specifications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No Reward Design (Task).</span>
This baseline does not utilize LLMs and uses only the task reward <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> and pseudo-reward <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> without incorporating any behavioral specifications (i.e., <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{H}=\tilde{r}_{L}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{H}=\tilde{r}_{L}=0</annotation></semantics></math>).
As this setting is less noisy, we run it for 5 trials.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2. </span>Domains</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the approaches on three long-horizon, multi-subtask domains: Rescue World, iTHOR, and Kitchen.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18582v1/figures/thor_pnp.png" id="S5.F4.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/389;" width="476" height="389" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S5.F4.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">iTHOR Domain</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18582v1/figures/kitchen.png" id="S5.F4.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:469/389;" width="469" height="389" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S5.F4.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Kitchen Domain</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>. </span><span id="S5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Rendered scenes from the iTHOR and Kitchen domains. Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (right) illustrates the Rescue World domain.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each domain poses distinct challenges in subtask sequencing and low-level execution.
Furthermore, as we see later, flat rewards cannot in principle capture all specifications in Rescue World and iTHOR, whereas they can in Kitchen.
This contrast allows us to investigate, <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">in practice</span>, how effectively language specifications can be translated into flat and hierarchical rewards across both types of scenarios.
Additional details are provided in the Appendix and Fig. <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.2. Domains ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rescue World.</span>
This is a variant of the Rescue World for Teams (RW4T) domain <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orlov Savko et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, where the agent must collect and deliver all supplies in the environment.
This domain features a large state space represented by a 407-dimensional vector and poses a long-horizon challenge, requiring the agent to complete 8 subtasks, each lasting up to around 10 steps.
Behavioral specifications include:
(1) a high-level <span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">persistence</span> specification for delivering all supplies of one type before switching to another and (2) a low-level <span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">safety</span> specification for avoiding hazardous zones while carrying supplies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">iTHOR.</span>
Built upon the Unity game engine, iTHOR is an environment within the AI2-THOR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kolve et al., 2017</a>)</cite> framework that features several realistic household scenes in which an agent navigates and interact with everyday objects.
Here, we focus on a long-horizon pick and place task within a kitchen setting consisting of 8 subtasks, each requiring up to approximately 30 steps to complete.
The agent must deliver a set of apples and eggs located on the dining table to the sink on the other side of the room.
The state space is represented by a 30-dimensional vector that contains object and agent positions and object states.
Behavioral specifications include: (1) a high-level <span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">diversity</span> specification that requires delivering a different item from the one previously delivered and (2) a low-level <span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">avoidance</span> specification that prevents the agent from going near a stool placed in the environment while picking up or delivering an egg.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Kitchen.</span>
This is a single-agent variant of Overcooked, an environment originally developed for studying human-AI collaboration in kitchen tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
In our setting, the agent needs to prepare a salad with lettuce, tomatoes, and onions.
This domain features an even larger state space, represented by a 699-dimensional continuous vector that captures various ingredient states.
It also involves a long-horizon task requiring the completion of 5 subtasks in a strict sequence, with the final 2 subtasks dependent on the successful completion of all preceding ones.
The high-level behavioral specification is a preferred <span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">chopping</span> sequence (e.g., tomatoes <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> onions <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> lettuce).
Since the environment uses fixed low-level policies, we skip low-level reward design in this domain.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3. </span>Numerical Experiments</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As a precursor to evaluting solutions to HRDL, we also conducted experiments where hand-crafted flat and hierarchical rewards were used directly to train policies <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">without requiring reward generation from language specifications</span>.
These experiments serve as a proof-of-concept and demonstrate that:</p>
<ul id="S5.I2" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S5.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">given expert-specified hierarchical rewards <math id="S5.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math>, existing RL algorithms can effectively learn hierarchical policies <math id="S5.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\pi_{H}^{*},\pi_{L}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\pi_{H}^{*},\pi_{L}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math> that achieve high task performance and strong alignment with designer specifications; and</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">while expert-specified flat rewards <math id="S5.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> can capture some behavioral specifications, they fail to express ones that require knowledge of the previous subtask (e.g., the <span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">persistence</span> specification in Rescue World and the <span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">diversity</span> specification in iTHOR).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We report these preliminary results in the Appendix.
Now, we return to the core HRDL setting, where designed rewards must be synthesized from natural language inputs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>. </span><span id="S5.T1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

</span></figcaption>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q1</span>. <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Are the designed rewards syntactically correct?</span>
Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.3. Numerical Experiments ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows that hierarchical reward generation achieves substantially lower code generation error rates than flat reward generation in all three domains, <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">suggesting that formulating the HRL reward design problem hierarchically can simplify reward synthesis for LLMs</span>.
In Rescue World and iTHOR, flat rewards cannot capture the high-level specifications, as doing so requires access to the previously executed option.
As a result, the LLM often hallucinates unavailable variables related to previously delivered object types.
In Kitchen, higher error rates stem from the complexity of reasoning over low-level actions.
For example, correctly checking if the agent is chopping an onion on the low-level requires inspecting coordinate-level state variables.
In contrast, having access to the options space in HRD enables direct reasoning over high-level behaviors (e.g., <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chop onion</span>), greatly simplifying reward generation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18582v1/figures/syntax_error.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:348/141;" width="348" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>. </span><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Syntax error rates for LLM-based reward generation, computed over 24 candidates per configuration.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q2</span>. <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Do the designed rewards preserve task feasibility?</span>
<span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> consistently better preserves task feasibility than <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> across all domains (Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.3. Numerical Experiments ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), which is essential for real-world deployment.
In Rescue World and iTHOR, flat rewards often rely on spurious heuristics to infer past behavior (e.g. inferring the last delivered item type from the agent’s current location), leading to unintended behaviors.
In iTHOR, flat rewards tend to misidentify the type of objects being picked up, resulting in incorrect reward accumulation.
In Kitchen, flat rewards frequently struggle to reason over low-level actions (e.g., which ingredient the agent is interacting with), producing alignment rewards that interfere with task completion.
Hierarchical rewards, by contrast, avoid these issues by conditioning on temporally extended options rather than raw state transitions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18582v1/figures/task_comp.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:348/143;" width="348" height="143" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>. </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Task completion rates for LLM-generated rewards, calculated as the proportion of designed rewards that preserve task feasibility among syntactically valid candidates.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q3</span>. <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Do the designed rewards actually lead to agent behavior that match the behavioral specifications?</span>
Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.3. Numerical Experiments ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes alignment performance using handcrafted high- and low-level ground-truth rewards <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Total</span> metric combines task and alignment rewards and serves as a proxy for the overall fitness <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math>.
In Rescue World, <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> substantially outperforms both <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Task</span> and <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> baselines on high-level alignment, achieving expert-level performance in 76.92% of successful runs.
This reflects its ability to encode the <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">persistence</span> specification, which flat rewards fundamentally cannot represent.
While <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> occasionally (12.50%) attains expert-level high-level alignment, these instances are coincidental.
Both methods perform comparably on low-level alignment, as the agent’s carrying status can be inferred from observable states without explicit option conditioning.
Overall, <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> achieves the highest total return, with 69.23% of policies attaining expert-level alignment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In iTHOR, <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> again outperforms <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> on high-level alignment, as the <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">diversity</span> specification cannot be fully captured by the flat reward without access to the agent’s current option.
In this case, <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> also significantly outperforms <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> on low-level alignment as well.
Although the LLM is explicitly asked to penalize the agent’s proximity to the stool when <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">on its way</span> to pick up or deliver, the generated flat rewards only apply the penalty in the timestep that the agent is specifically performing the pick or place action, leading the agent to not avoid the stool.
This makes sense, as it is difficult to discern the agent’s intent in picking up or dropping an egg from just the state without option information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In Kitchen, <span id="S5.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> achieves substantially higher alignment with the chopping specification (92.86% vs. 10.00%).
Although flat rewards are theoretically capable of encoding this behavior, doing so requires complex and brittle logic: only 1 flat reward candidate successfully implemented the specification.
This demonstrates a key advantage of designing rewards for HRL with HRD: even when flat rewards are theoretically sufficient, hierarchical rewards can simplify reward design through high-level abstractions and lead to better alignment with behavioral specifications.
Example videos of policies for all domains are provided in the supplementary material.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4. </span>Evaluations with Human Participants</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In real-world applications, manually designed ground-truth rewards are rarely available.
To better reflect practical deployment scenarios, we conducted an IRB-approved user study on Rescue World and Kitchen using human participants recruited via Prolific.
The goal was to assess whether <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> agents are perceived as better aligned with behavioral specifications than <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this study, non-expert participants effectively served the role of fitness function <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math>, providing human-centered evaluations.
Participants viewed videos of agent behaviors produced by both methods and rated their alignment with textual specifications on a scale from 1 (least aligned) to 5 (most aligned), similar to the scale employed in the evaluation methodology of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Participants were not aware of the underlying reward design methods of the policies.
We collected usable responses (e.g., those that passed attention checks) from 30 participants, evenly split across the two domains.
Further details of the study design are provided in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18582v1/figures/human_ratings2.png" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:443/214;" width="443" height="214" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>. </span><span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Human-provided ratings for agent alignment.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Fig. <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.4. Evaluations with Human Participants ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, participants consistently rated <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> agents higher than <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> for high-level alignment.
In Rescue World, <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> significantly outperforms <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> on the <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">persistence</span> preference (4.76 vs. 2.42), a specification that flat rewards struggle to capture due to the lack of previous option information.
While both methods have similar ratings for the low-level <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">safety</span> specification, <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> achieves significantly higher <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">overall</span> alignment scores (4.64 vs. 3.46).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In Kitchen, the advantage of <span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> is even more pronounced for the <span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">chopping</span> specification (4.47 vs. 1.70).
This larger gap arises because, unlike in Rescue World, the preferred behavior in Kitchen rarely occurs accidentally,
as aligning with the <span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">chopping</span> specification requires taking additional steps in the environment.
Notably, across both domains, <span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> policies consistently receive average ratings above 4, indicating a strong perception of alignment.
These findings suggest that, in practice, when task completion is used to filter out unsuccessful policies, the remaining <span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> candidates are consistently well-aligned with behavioral specifications.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>. </span><span id="S5.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Candidate agent policies (%) that received a perfect alignment score from all human participants.</span></figcaption>
<div id="S5.T2.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:162.2pt;height:25.6pt;vertical-align:-11.5pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-75.8pt,12.0pt) scale(0.516811427045175,0.516811427045175) ;">
<table id="S5.T2.5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">

<div id="S5.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.4. Evaluations with Human Participants ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that over half of the policies produced by <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> achieve perfect human ratings across all behavioral specifications, substantially outperforming those generated by <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span>.
Overall, <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> consistently outperforms <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> in capturing language-based behavioral specifications across domains in both simulated evaluations and user studies.</p>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6. </span>Conclusion</h3>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper introduces the <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hierarchical Reward Design (HRD) problem</span>, which (1) formulates a more expressive reward structure than flat rewards, (2) integrates seamlessly with existing decision-making frameworks and RL algorithms, and (3) better encodes behavioral specifications for long-horizon tasks, with an initial solution to this problem (<span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">L2HR</span>) achieving considerably better or comparable results in both numerical and human evaluations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While our results provide strong motivation for HRD, several limitations and interesting areas for future investigation remain.
First, our experiments focus on complex but simulated domains; evaluating HRD in real-world settings, such as robotics and interactive AI systems, is an important next step.
Second, more advanced reward generation techniques, including evolutionary optimization or human feedback, may further improve performance.
Finally, since option discovery remains a core challenge in Hierarchical RL, jointly addressing option discovery and reward design could substantially enhance practical applicability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, <span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">we emphasize that human-agent alignment is inherently challenging and HRD should not be viewed in isolation</span>.
Rather, it complements a broader ecosystem of alignment approaches, including learning from demonstrations, rankings, and user corrections.
Understanding how HRDL and L2HR interact with these approaches is an important avenue for future work, bringing us closer to AI agents that are reliably aligned with human needs, values and objectives.</p>
</div>
