</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.T3" title="In D.2. Results with Expert-Provided Rewards ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports the results of policies trained with expert-provided flat <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and hierarchical rewards <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{H}^{*},\tilde{r}_{L}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math> (shown in the table as <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat*</span> and <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> respectively).
In other words, no LLMs were used for reward generation in these experiments.
Across all three domains (Rescue World, iTHOR, and Kitchen), <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> consistently achieves the highest total returns.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In Rescue World, <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> matches <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat*</span> in low-level alignment return but significantly outperforms it in high-level alignment, achieving an average total return of 97.15 with 80.00% policies reaching expert alignment, compared to 85.88 and 0.00% for <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat*</span>.
A similar pattern is observed in iTHOR, where <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> achieves an average total return of 42.61 with all policies reaching expert alignment, while <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat*</span> achieves 35.41 with none reaching expert alignment.
We also note that although <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat*</span> matched <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> in low-level alignment for iTHOR, it did so by following the low-level <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">avoidance</span> preference regardless of the option.
In contrast, <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> selectively applies this preference to options involving eggs, demonstrating finer-grained alignment with low-level human specifications.
These results highlight that <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> better captures behavioral dependencies related to the current and previous options, enabling it to represent high-level <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">persistence</span> in Rescue World and <span id="A4.SS2.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">diversity</span> in iTHOR, which are beyond the representational capacity of flat rewards.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In Kitchen, <span id="A4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier*</span> and <span id="A4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat*</span> perform equally well on both task and high-level returns.
While <span id="A4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat*</span> is theoretically capable of capturing dependencies on the previous subtask in Kitchen by inferring it from environment state, doing so is difficult and error-prone without expert-designed rewards, as shown in Sec. <a href="#S5" title="5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
Overall, these results demonstrate that expert-designed hierarchical rewards can be easily integrated with task-related rewards to train policies that (1) achieve strong task performance comparable to baselines without reward design (2) align well with behavioral specifications, including those that flat rewards cannot effectively represent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3. </span>Training Setup</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our implementation, we used LLMs to generate <span id="A4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">single-step</span> high-level rewards, allowing the high-level decision process to be modeled as either an MDP or an SMDP.
When using an SMDP, we computed the corresponding SMDP rewards using Eq. <a href="#A2.E8" title="Equation 8 ‣ B.1.3. High-Level MDP Model ‣ B.1. Low- and High-Level Decision Models ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.3.2. </span>iTHOR</h5>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For iTHOR, we modeled the high-level decision-making as an SMDP and trained the high-level policy <math id="A4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{H}</annotation></semantics></math> using DQN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mnih et al., 2015</a>)</cite>.
The hyperparameters for training <math id="A4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{H}</annotation></semantics></math> are as follows:</p>

</div></li>
<li id="A4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<section id="A4.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.3.3. </span>Kitchen</h5>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For Kitchen, we modeled the high-level decision-making as an MDP and trained the high-level policy <math id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{H}</annotation></semantics></math> using DQN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mnih et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, implemented so that termination conditions <math id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> were enforced during rollouts.
We adopted the MDP formulation because it outperformed the SMDP setting with DQN in this domain.
Given the highly delayed rewards and the importance of subtask sequencing in Kitchen, we also incorporated specification-agnostic demonstrations to bootstrap policy learning.
Hyperparameters for learning the high-level policy <math id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{H}</annotation></semantics></math> are as follows:</p>

<div id="A4.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Network: 2 layers with 256 units each and ReLU non-linearities</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A4.I5.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A4.I5.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.I5.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Optimizer: Adam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Ba, 2014</a>)</cite></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A4.I5.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<p id="A4.I5.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Learning rate: <math id="A4.I5.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\cdot 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\cdot 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math> with linear scheduling</p>
</div></li>

</div></li>
<li id="A4.I5.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A4.I5.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.I5.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Total timesteps: <math id="A4.I5.i6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\cdot 10^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\cdot 10^{6}</annotation></semantics></math></p>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For Rescue World and Kitchen, we used a server with 30 vCPUs and an NVIDIA A10 GPU (24GB PCIe) to train <math id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> policies in parallel, each corresponding to one of the <math id="A4.SS3.SSS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> reward candidates generated by the LLM. For iTHOR, we used a server with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU to train our policies.</p>

<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4. </span>LLM Prompts</h4>

<div id="A4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prompts used in our work are adapted from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, but differ in important ways to realize hierarchical rewards.
Specifically, our prompts are designed to:
(1) reflect a hierarchical reward structure; and
(2) generate rewards that align with behavioral specifications while preserving task feasibility.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.4.1. </span>System Prompt</h5>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, our system prompt provides a concise, domain-agnostic description of the reward design task and defines the function signature that the LLM should use in its output.
The full system prompt is provided in Prompt 1 on <a href="#A4.SS4.SSS2" title="D.4.2. User Prompt ‣ D.4. LLM Prompts ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.4.2. </span>User Prompt</h5>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The user prompts follow a similar methodology to that of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, using code snippets as contextual input and an accompanying task-specific natural language description.
To support hierarchical reward generation, we extend the accompanying task description by providing the following: (1) a description of relevant action spaces (i.e., the option space <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> and/or action space <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>) to help the LLM distinguish between temporally extended behaviors and primitive actions; (2) a behavioral specification describing preferences beyond task completion; (3) additional code formatting guidelines to emphasize that the LLM should capture behavioral logic without making the reward function stateful (e.g., storing variables across calls).
Moreover, the complexity of our domains introduces two additional challenges, which we address by augmenting the code snippets with further contextual information:</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-file Dependencies.</span>
In our environments, key components of the task logic often depend on constants and definitions from separate supporting files (e.g., <span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">utils.py</span>).
To address this, we manually copied the necessary definitions from these files and included them as background comments at the top of the environment code provided to the LLM.
This ensures all relevant constants and definitions are explicitly exposed during reward generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Complex Observation Representations.</span>
Our environments feature structured observations, such as spatial maps, whose semantics are not fully captured by the observation’s shape or naming alone.
For example, it can be difficult to infer what each value in the observation (e.g., map cell) represents from the environment code.
To mitigate this, we also provided an example observation input as part of the background comments in cases where the LLM might find it challenging to correctly interpret the structure and meaning of the observation space.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure a fair comparison across conditions, the same code snippets of each domain were used for all reward generation tasks, whether generating low-level, high-level, or flat rewards.
The full environment contexts and corresponding prompts for both Rescue World and Kitchen are shown in Prompt 2 and Prompt 3 on <a href="#A4.SS4.SSS2" title="D.4.2. User Prompt ‣ D.4. LLM Prompts ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4.2</span></a> and <a href="#A4.SS4.SSS2" title="D.4.2. User Prompt ‣ D.4. LLM Prompts ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4.2</span></a> respectively.</p>
</div>

<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p5.pic1.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p5.pic1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The output of the reward function should consist of two items: 
<br class="ltx_break">(1) the user preference reward, 
<br class="ltx_break">(2) a dictionary of each individual reward component in the user preference reward. 
<br class="ltx_break">The code output should be formatted as a python code string: "python … ".</span></span>
<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p5.pic1.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p5.pic1.2.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Some helpful tips for writing the reward function code: 
<br class="ltx_break">(1) Most importantly, the reward code’s input variables must contain only attributes of the provided environment class definition (namely, variables that have prefix self.). Under no circumstance can you introduce new input variables.</span></span>

<br class="ltx_break"></span></span>
<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p6.pic1.p1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p6.pic1.p1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The LLM receives one of the prompts below, chosen according to the reward function we want it to design.
The prompt for each setting is identical except for (1) descriptions of relevant task spaces (e.g., the flat-reward prompt omits the options space description) and (2) the behavioral specification (“user preference”) string.<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p6.pic1.p1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span>

<section id="A4.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">High-Level</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to deliver all objects on the map.
In the task reward, the agent gets a reward of +30 when it successfully delivers an object,
and a step cost of -1 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s option/subtask (referred to as HL_Action in the code) space consists of going to and delivering the two types of objects.
Each option takes multiple action steps to complete.
Taking a ’go to’ option means that the agent will navigate to a supply and pick it up.
Taking a ’deliver’ option means that the agent will navigate to the delivery location and drop the object.
Note that the agent has to first go to the object to pick it up before delivering the object.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should pick up an object type that’s the same as the previously delivered object type,
if there are still objects of that type remaining in the environment.
Otherwise, the agent should pick up an object of a different type.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You need to write a reward function to encode this user preference.
The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.
Please make sure NOT to make the reward function stateful (i.e. you should not use function attributes or global variables.)
You should also not write any other helper functions.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                        
<section id="A4.SSx2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Low-Level</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to deliver all objects on the map.
In the task reward, the agent gets a reward of +30 when it successfully delivers an object,
and a step cost of -1 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s option/subtask (referred to as HL_Action in the code) space consists of going to and delivering the two types of objects.
Each option takes multiple action steps to complete.
Taking a ’go to’ option means that the agent will navigate to a supply and pick it up.
Taking a ’deliver’ option means that the agent will navigate to the delivery location and drop the object.
Note that the agent has to first go to the object to pick it up before delivering the object.
The agent’s action (referred to as LL_Action in the code) space consists of moving in the four cardinal directions, as well as atomic actions pick and drop.
The agent can only perform LL_Action "pick" if it is at the same location as the object.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should avoid yellow danger zones when it is delivering an object.
However, the agent does not need to avoid danger zones when it is going to an object.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You need to write a reward function to encode this user preference.
The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.
Please make sure NOT to make the reward function stateful (i.e. you should not use function attributes or global variables.)
You should also not write any other helper functions.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                        
<section id="A4.SSx3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Flat</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to deliver all objects on the map.
In the task reward, the agent gets a reward of +30 when it successfully delivers an object,
and a step cost of -1 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s action (referred to as LL_Action in the code) space consists of moving in the four cardinal directions, as well as atomic actions pick and drop.
The agent can only perform LL_Action "pick" if it is at the same location as the object.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should pick up an object type that’s the same as the previously delivered object type,

In addition, the agent should avoid yellow danger zones when it is delivering an object.
However, the agent does not need to avoid danger zones when it is going to an object.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>

The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.
Please make sure NOT to make the reward function stateful (i.e. you should not use function attributes or global variables.)
You should also not write any other helper functions.</span></span>

<br class="ltx_break"></span></span>
<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.pic1.p1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.pic1.p1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The LLM receives one of the prompts below, chosen according to the reward function we want it to design.
The prompt for each setting is identical except for (1) descriptions of relevant task spaces (e.g., the flat-reward prompt omits the options space description) and (2) the behavioral specification (“user preference”) string.<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.pic1.p1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span>

<section id="A4.SSx4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">High-Level</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to pick up all apples and eggs on the dining table and place them in the sink.
In the task reward, the agent gets a reward of +10 after it successfully picks up an object and places it in the sink, and a step cost of -0.1 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s option/subtask (referred to as self.pnp_hl_actions in the code) space consists of picking up and placing the two types of objects.
Each option takes multiple action steps to complete.
Taking a ’pick’ option means that the agent will navigate to an object and pick it up.
Taking a ’place’ option means that the agent will navigate to the delivery location and place the object there.
Note that the agent has to first go to the object to pick it up before placing the object.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should pick up an object type that’s different from the previously placed object type, as long as there are objects of the other type on the table need to be picked.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You need to write a reward function to encode this user preference.
The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.
It can take up to 30 steps to reach an object and pick it up, or to reach the sink and drop it off.
Make sure your reward scaling gives the preference for alternating objects much more weight than the negative step rewards, but still lower than the positive task reward.
Please make sure NOT to make the reward function stateful (i.e. you should not use function attributes or global variables).
You should also not write any other helper functions.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                        
<section id="A4.SSx5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Low-Level</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to pick up all apples and eggs on the dining table and place them in the sink.
In the task reward, the agent gets a reward of +10 after it successfully picks up an object and places it in the sink, and a step cost of -0.1 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s option/subtask (referred to as self.pnp_hl_actions in the code) space consists of picking up and placing the two types of objects.
Each option takes multiple action steps to complete.
Taking a ’pick’ option means that the agent will navigate to an object and pick it up.
Taking a ’place’ option means that the agent will navigate to the delivery location and place the object there.
Note that the agent has to first go to the object to pick it up before placing the object. The agent’s action (referred to as self.pnp_ll_actions in the code) space consists of the primitives for: moving forward, rotating left, rotating right, picking up the closest object, and placing a held object in receptacle.
The agent can only perform the low level pick or place primitive only if the agent is close enough to an object or a receptacle.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should avoid the stool in the environment both when it is on its way to pick up an egg and place an egg down.
More specifically, the agent should be penalized when it is within 1.5 meters of the stool.
However, the agent does not need to avoid the stool when it is on its way to pick up an apple or place an apple down.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx5.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You need to write a reward function to encode this user preference.
The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.

<section id="A4.SSx6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Flat</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to pick up all apples and eggs on the dining table and place them in the sink.
In the task reward, the agent gets a reward of +10 after it successfully picks up an object and places it in the sink, and a step cost of -0.1 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx6.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s action (referred to as self.pnp_ll_actions in the code) space consists of the primitives for: moving forward, rotating left, rotating right, picking up the closest object, and placing a held object in receptacle.
The agent can only perform the low level pick or place primitive only if the agent is close enough to an object or a receptacle.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx6.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should avoid the stool in the environment both when it is on its way to pick up an egg and place an egg down.
More specifically, the agent should be penalized when it is within 1.5 meters of the stool.
However, the agent does not need to avoid the stool when it is on its way to pick up an apple or place an apple down. In addition, the agent should pick up an object type that’s different from the previously placed object type, as long as there are objects of the other type on the table need to be picked.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx6.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx6.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You need to write a reward function to encode this user preference.
The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.
It can take up to 30 steps to reach an object and pick it up, or to reach the sink and drop it off.
Make sure your reward scaling gives the preference for alternating objects much more weight than the negative step rewards, but still lower than the positive task reward.
Please make sure NOT to make the reward function stateful (i.e. you should not use function attributes or global variables.)
You should also not write any other helper functions.</span></span>
</span>
</section>

<br class="ltx_break"></span></span>
<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p8.pic1.p1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p8.pic1.p1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The LLM receives one of the prompts below, chosen according to the reward function we want it to design.
The prompt for each setting is identical except for (1) descriptions of relevant task spaces (e.g., the flat-reward prompt omits the options space description) and (2) the behavioral specification (“user preference”) string.<span id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p8.pic1.p1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span>

<section id="A4.SSx7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">High-Level</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to prepare one David’s salad with three ingredients: onion, lettuce, and tomatoes.
To make this salad, the agent needs to:
a. Chop ingredients (onion, lettuce, and tomatoes).
Only one ingredient of each type is needed to complete the salad.
b. Combined chopped ingredients.
c. Plate the salad.
The task reward already encodes the task objective.
In the task rewrd, the agent receives a reward of +1 when it completes a salad, and a step cost of -0.01 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx7.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s option (subtask) space consists of macro cooking actions, such as ’Chop Onion’ and ’Plate David Salad’.
Each option takes multiple action steps to complete.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx7.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx7.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should chop an onion after it chops a tomato, and the agent should chop a lettuce after it chops an onion.
If the ingredients are already chopped or a combined salad already exists, the agent should not chop more ingredients.
The mixing order of the ingredients does not matter.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx7.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx7.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx7.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You need to write a reward function to encode this user preference.
The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.
Please make sure NOT to make the reward function stateful (i.e. you should not use function attributes or global variables.)
You should also not write any other helper functions.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                        
<section id="A4.SSx8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Flat</h4>

<span id="A4.SSx8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task description:</span><span id="A4.SSx8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx8.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The task objective is to prepare one David’s salad with three ingredients: onion, lettuce, and tomatoes.
To make this salad, the agent needs to:
a. Chop ingredients (onion, lettuce, and tomatoes).
Only one ingredient of each type is needed to complete the salad.
b. Combined chopped ingredients.
c. Plate the salad.
The task reward already encodes the task objective.
In the task reward, the agent receives a reward of +1 when it completes a salad, and a step cost of -0.01 for each time step taken.
The reward function you write does not need to encode the task objective.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx8.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relevant task spaces:</span><span id="A4.SSx8.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx8.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent’s action (low-level action) space consists of moving in the four cardinal directions (up, down, left, right) and idle.
When an agent is standing next to a counter, performing an action in the direction of the counter interacts with the counter.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx8.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx8.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">User preference:</span><span id="A4.SSx8.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx8.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The agent should chop an onion after it chops a tomato, and the agent should chop a lettuce after it chops an onion.
If the ingredients are already chopped or a combined salad already exists, the agent should not chop more ingredients.
The mixing order of the ingredients does not matter.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A4.SSx8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A4.SSx8.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SSx8.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional info:</span><span id="A4.SSx8.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.SSx8.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You need to write a reward function to encode this user preference.
The preference function you write will be used together with the task reward to train the agent.
Please make sure NOT to make the reward function stateful (i.e. you should not use function attributes or global variables.)
You should also not write any other helper functions.</span></span>

<span id="lstnumberx779" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx779.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">        </span><span id="lstnumberx779.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">reward</span><span id="lstnumberx779.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx779.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">+=</span><span id="lstnumberx779.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx779.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">0.5</span>

<span id="lstnumberx780" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx780.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">        </span><span id="lstnumberx780.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">reward_components</span><span id="lstnumberx780.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">[</span><span id="lstnumberx780.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_string" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">"lettuce_after_onion"</span><span id="lstnumberx780.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">]</span><span id="lstnumberx780.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx780.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">=</span><span id="lstnumberx780.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx780.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">0.5</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx781" class="ltx_listingline">
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx782" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx782.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    </span><span id="lstnumberx782.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_comment ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">#<span id="lstnumberx782.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>Avoid<span id="lstnumberx782.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>chopping<span id="lstnumberx782.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>ingredients<span id="lstnumberx782.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>again<span id="lstnumberx782.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>if<span id="lstnumberx782.2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>they<span id="lstnumberx782.2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>are<span id="lstnumberx782.2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>already<span id="lstnumberx782.2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>chopped</span>

</span>
<span id="lstnumberx784" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx784.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">       </span><span id="lstnumberx784.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(</span><span id="lstnumberx784.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">option</span><span id="lstnumberx784.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx784.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">==</span><span id="lstnumberx784.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx784.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">CHOP_ONION</span><span id="lstnumberx784.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx784.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">and</span><span id="lstnumberx784.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx784.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">onion_chopped</span><span id="lstnumberx784.12" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">)</span><span id="lstnumberx784.13" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx784.14" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">or</span><span id="lstnumberx784.15" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx784.16" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">\</span>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>User Study Details</h3>

<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1. </span>Experiment Protocol</h4>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted a user study to evaluate how well agent policies trained with hierarchical rewards (experimental group) generated by language models are perceived to align with given behavioral specifications compared to those trained with flat rewards (control group), also generated using language models.
Each participant was randomly assigned to either the Rescue World or Kitchen domain.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="A5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="A5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1)</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Consent and Study Overview.</span>
Participants were first presented with a detailed overview of the study, including its purpose, procedures, and any potential risks.
An IRB-approved consent form was provided, and participants were required to give informed consent before proceeding.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2)</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Demographic Questionnaire.</span>
After providing consent, participants completed a brief demographic questionnaire, where we asked for their age and sex.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(3)</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Domain Introduction.</span>
Participants were introduced to the assigned domain through textual descriptions accompanied by screenshots.
This step was designed to ensure that they had sufficient context to understand the environment and the tasks performed by the agent.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(4)</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Presentation of Behavioral Specifications and Attention Checks.</span>
Next, participants were shown the behavioral specifications the agent was expected to follow.
To ensure they carefully read these specifications, we included attention check questions.
For example, in the Rescue World domain, where the agent must handle two object types (food and medical kits) and may encounter avoid danger zones (marked by yellow grids), part of the <span id="A5.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">safety</span> specification states that the robot should “avoid yellow danger zones when it is delivering an object”.
We asked participants, whether according to the specifications, it would be considered safe for the robot to “go through danger zones while delivering food”.
While participants were not required to answer these questions correctly to proceed, we filtered out all responses with incorrect answers during data analysis to ensure data quality.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(5)</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Video Evaluation.</span>
To ensure consistent evaluation, only policies that successfully completed the task were shown.
Additionally, to control for variability, all videos shown to a participant were drawn from policies trained with the same random seed, although they could originate from different reward candidates.
In the <span id="A5.I1.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Rescue World</span> domain, each participant viewed 6 videos: 3 showing policies trained with flat rewards <math id="A5.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{r}_{flat}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{r}_{flat}</annotation></semantics></math> and 3 showing policies trained with hierarchical rewards <math id="A5.I1.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{r}_{H},\tilde{r}_{L})</annotation></semantics></math>.
In the <span id="A5.I1.i5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Kitchen</span> domain, participants viewed 4 videos: 2 per reward method. Fewer videos were shown in this domain because, in some cases, only 2 out of 8 flat reward candidates produced policies capable of successfully completing the task.
Questions for each video appeared on the same page, and participants were allowed to replay the videos as many times as they wished.
After each video, participants first answered a multiple-choice question to verify they had watched the video (e.g., “What order did the robot deliver the objects in?”).
They were then asked to rate how well the agent’s behavior aligned with the specified behaviors using a 5-point scale, with 1 indicating “least aligned” and 5 indicating “most aligned”.
Participants could optionally provide any comments explaining their ratings.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(6)</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Final Feedback and Compensation.</span>
At the end of the study, participants were invited to leave any additional feedback about their experience.
On average, participants took 14.2 minutes to complete the study (SD = 8.7 minutes).
All participants who completed the full study were compensated $3 for their time.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2. </span>Participants</h4>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted the user study on Prolific, recruiting a total of 40 participants from the United States.
After applying attention check filters, we obtained usable data from 30 participants, with 15 participants assigned to each domain.
Among these 30 participants, the youngest was 20, the oldest was 67, and the median age was 35.
The sex distribution was fairly balanced, with 14 female participants, 15 male participants, and 1 participant identifying as “non-binary / third gender.”</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3. </span>Data Analysis</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We filtered out data from participants who incorrectly answered the attention check questions about the behavioral specifications.
For participants who passed the attention checks, if they answered a video content question incorrectly, we excluded their ratings for that specific video but retained their responses for other videos.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To generate Fig. <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.4. Evaluations with Human Participants ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Reward Design from Language: Enhancing Alignment of Agent Behavior with Human Specifications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, we computed the average rating each participant assigned to <span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> and <span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> policies, and then aggregated these per-participant means to report group-level comparisons.
Since each participant evaluated both <span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flat</span> and <span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hier</span> policies trained with the same random seed, we used the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test to assess the statistical significance of the observed rating differences <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffman and Zhao, 2020</a>)</cite>.
All reported results are based on the filtered dataset, with the final sample sizes specified in the Participants section.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>

    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
